question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what should each operator do?
choice_a: The larger vessel always has the right of way and the smaller vessel must always be first to turn
choice_b: Each should turn to port (left) to pass starboard-to-starboard
choice_c: Each should alter course to starboard (right) so the vessels pass port-to-port, like cars passing on a road
choice_d: Both vessels should stop and wait for radio instructions
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the Navigation Rules direct both power-driven vessels to alter course to starboard so they pass safely port side to port side, similar to the convention of driving on the right.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 14, head-on situation), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'give-way' vessel that must take early and substantial action to avoid a collision?
choice_a: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching from its own port (left) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching from its own starboard (right) side
explanation: In a crossing situation, the vessel that sees the other vessel on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must take early, obvious action -- typically slowing or turning to pass behind the other boat's stern -- while the other vessel is the stand-on vessel and should maintain course and speed.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 15, crossing situation), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: What is the responsibility of the 'stand-on' vessel in a meeting, crossing, or overtaking situation?
choice_a: Maintain its current course and speed so the give-way vessel can predict its movement, while remaining ready to take action if a collision becomes imminent
choice_b: Immediately stop the engine and drop anchor
choice_c: Speed up to get out of the way as fast as possible
choice_d: Turn hard to port regardless of the situation
explanation: The stand-on vessel should hold its course and speed so the give-way vessel can maneuver predictably around it, but must still take whatever action is necessary -- including stopping -- if the give-way vessel fails to act and collision becomes unavoidable.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, stand-on vessel duties), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: When one vessel is overtaking another (approaching from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the other's beam), which vessel must keep clear?
choice_a: Neither vessel needs to take any action in an overtaking situation
choice_b: The overtaking vessel must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken, no matter what type of vessel either one is
choice_c: The vessel being overtaken must always turn out of the way
choice_d: Right-of-way in overtaking situations depends only on which vessel is larger
explanation: Regardless of vessel type, an overtaking vessel is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel it is passing until it is well clear ahead, since the overtaken vessel may not be able to see it easily.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 13, overtaking), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: In general, which vessel has the right of way over a power-driven vessel: a sailing vessel under sail alone, or a vessel engaged in commercial fishing with gear deployed?
choice_a: Right-of-way is decided strictly by which vessel arrived on the water first that day
choice_b: Sailing vessels never have right-of-way over any powered vessel
choice_c: Both a sailing vessel under sail alone and a vessel restricted by fishing gear generally have right-of-way over an ordinary power-driven vessel, since power-driven vessels have more maneuverability
choice_d: A power-driven pleasure boat always has the right of way over both sailboats and fishing vessels
explanation: The general right-of-way hierarchy gives way to vessels that are less maneuverable: an ordinary power-driven vessel must generally give way to a sailing vessel under sail alone and to a vessel actively engaged in fishing with gear deployed that restricts its ability to maneuver.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, general right-of-way hierarchy, Rule 18), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: How should a vessel operator behave when navigating in a narrow channel or fairway?
choice_a: Travel down the exact center of the channel at all times
choice_b: Always give way to any vessel exiting a marina, regardless of channel position
choice_c: Channels have no special navigation rules different from open water
choice_d: Keep as far to the outer edge of the channel that lies on the vessel's starboard side as is safe and practicable, and avoid crossing in a way that impedes vessels that can only navigate safely within the channel
explanation: In a narrow channel, vessels should keep to the starboard side of the channel and avoid impeding larger vessels, such as deep-draft ships, that are constrained to the channel because they cannot safely navigate outside it.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 9, narrow channels), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula, relevant to Massachusetts harbor and channel traffic

question: What does one long horn blast typically indicate in Massachusetts harbors and channels, such as when a vessel is approaching a blind bend?
choice_a: A warning signal alerting other vessels to the operator's presence, often used when visibility around a bend or obstruction is limited
choice_b: A request for another vessel to stop its engine immediately
choice_c: A signal that the vessel is anchoring for the night
choice_d: A greeting with no navigational meaning
explanation: A single prolonged blast is used as a warning signal, including when approaching a bend or obstruction with limited visibility, so vessels on the other side are alerted to a vessel's presence before it comes into view.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 34, sound signals), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: What do the International and U.S. Inland Navigation Rules require every vessel to maintain at all times?
choice_a: A lookout is only required at night
choice_b: A proper lookout by sight and hearing, using all available means appropriate to the conditions, to fully assess risk of collision
choice_c: A continuous radio broadcast of the vessel's position
choice_d: A lookout is only required for vessels over 65 feet
explanation: Rule 5 requires every vessel to keep a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times, using all available means suited to the circumstances, so the risk of collision can be properly assessed regardless of vessel size or time of day.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 5, lookout), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: What is meant by operating at a 'safe speed' under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: A fixed speed of 5 mph that applies on all waters at all times
choice_b: Any speed, as long as the vessel remains within a marked channel
choice_c: A speed that allows a vessel to take proper and effective action to avoid collision and stop within a distance appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions, such as visibility, traffic density, and sea state
choice_d: The maximum speed the engine is physically capable of producing
explanation: Safe speed is not a fixed number; it depends on visibility, traffic, sea and weather conditions, and the vessel's maneuverability, and requires being able to stop or take avoiding action in time given those conditions.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 6, safe speed), consistent with NASBLA-aligned course curricula

question: What should a boater do when encountering a large commercial vessel, ferry, or ship in a Massachusetts harbor channel, such as Boston Harbor?
choice_a: Cut directly in front of it since recreational vessels generally have the right of way
choice_b: Match its speed and travel directly alongside as closely as possible
choice_c: Ignore it since collision rules do not apply to commercial traffic
choice_d: Stay well clear and give it a wide berth, since large deep-draft vessels have limited maneuverability, longer stopping distances, and large blind spots close to the bow
explanation: Large commercial vessels and ferries cannot stop or turn quickly, and often cannot see small recreational boats close to their bow; smaller vessels should stay well clear and never assume they can outmaneuver or cross closely in front of a ship in a busy harbor like Boston Harbor.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (large-vessel encounter safety), relevant to Massachusetts's commercial harbor traffic (Boston Harbor, New Bedford, etc.)

question: In restricted visibility such as fog, what must a power-driven vessel making way through the water sound on its whistle?
choice_a: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than two minutes
choice_b: Three short blasts every ten seconds
choice_c: No sound signal is required in fog if radar is aboard
explanation: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel underway and making way must sound one prolonged blast at intervals of no more than two minutes, alerting nearby vessels to its presence when it cannot be seen.
source_note: Universal boating safety fundamentals (U.S. Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 35, sound signals in restricted visibility), particularly relevant to Massachusetts's frequent coastal fog
